newsitem.title: MEXICO: Gabriel Figueroa, 90, giant of Mexican cinema, dies.
newsitem.headline: Gabriel Figueroa, 90, giant of Mexican cinema, dies.

text.p: Gabriel Figueroa, a pioneering cinematographer in Mexico who also worked with top U.S. directors like John Huston and John Ford, died of a stroke following heart surgery, family members said on Monday.
Figueroa, who was 90, died on Sunday. He was to receive special honours on Monday at the Bellas Artes museum and theatre in central Mexico City.

He was one of the last survivors of Mexico's golden film era during the 1930s and 1940s, leaving only a handful of figures like screen star Maria Felix, a captivating beauty who symblized the times, and Ismael Rodriguez, who directed the late Pedro Infante, Mexico's version of the singing cowboy.
Figueroa's trademark was the spectacular landscape, dramatically depicting Mexican skies and deserts in establishing shots. "Figueroa skies" became internationally renowned in the film industry.

In the 1930s, Figueroa studied under the famous U.S. cinemotographer Gray Toland in Hollywood, where he developed the "deep focus" technique permitting complex compositions. He worked with Huston on "Night of the Iguana" (1955) and "Under the Volcano" (1984) and with Ford on "The Fugitive" (1947).

In Mexico, Don Gaby, as he was known affectionately, was best known for his work on "La Noche de Los Mayas" in 1939, which the government news agency Notimex said was the only work with which he was totally satisfied.

Other of his landmark Mexican films included "Maria Candelaria" (1943), which was honoured at Cannes, "Alla en el Rancho Grande" (1936), and "La Perla" (1947), a Spanish-language version of John Steinbeck's "The Pearl."
He began studying still photography at age 16 but was not considered much of a talent at the studio where he worked and was relegated to the laboratory, Notimex said.

Rather than being discouraged, Figueroa dedicated himself more to his craft, finally earning a break when he was discovered by Gilberto Martinez Solares, a director of Pedro Infante films, who introduced him to Alex Phillips, a top cinematographer who helped him get his first job in the industry.
